# snap-stanford/biomni (commit 400c1f366b96a35ca253e13c9b06c5076af41d65)
# snap-stanford/biomni Overview
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) project implements an AI agent for autonomous biomedical research, integrating large language models with retrieval-augmented planning and code execution. It orchestrates various AI agents to manage research tasks, dynamically handle resources, and engage in conversational interactions to solve complex biomedical problems.

The system's architecture centers on agent orchestration. A primary agent, [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56), manages the overall workflow, handling configuration, setting up language models, and dynamically managing tools and data. Its operational flow uses a [`StateGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L15) for iterative planning, execution, and observation. A complementary ReAct agent uses [`LangGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L265) to manage conversational state, integrate language models, and dynamically invoke tools. Further details on agent architecture are available in [Biomni Agent (A1) Architecture and Workflow](#project-overview-and-core-components-biomni-agent-a1-architecture-and-workflow) and [ReAct Agent Implementation and State Management](#project-overview-and-core-components-react-agent-implementation-and-state-management).

Language model integration allows various LLMs from different providers to be configured and used through a factory function. This enables dynamic imports and provider-specific configurations. The system includes a [`FunctionGenerator`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py#L22) agent that translates natural language into executable Python code. Utility functions support safe and efficient execution across languages like R and Bash. For more information, see [LLM Integration and Configuration](#project-overview-and-core-components-llm-integration-and-configuration) and [Code Generation and Execution](#project-overview-and-core-components-code-generation-and-execution).

Dynamic resource management and retrieval are key features. The [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8) intelligently selects relevant tools, data lake items, software libraries, and know-how documents based on user queries. This process uses LLM prompt-based selection to inform the agent's context. [Dynamic Resource Management and Retrieval](#project-overview-and-core-components-dynamic-resource-management-and-retrieval) provides additional details.

[`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) provides an array of tools and resources for biomedical analyses. These include a comprehensive suite of domain-specific tools, organized by scientific discipline. It also manages a collection of structured know-how documents and protocols. [Biomedical Tools and Resources](#biomedical-tools-and-resources) further describes these capabilities.

A specialized bioinformatics environment is required for [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25)'s operations. Shell scripts manage [`conda`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L30) and [`micromamba`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L21) installations, integrate core bioinformatics tools, and configure command-line interface tools. These scripts handle error conditions and ensure proper environment activation and [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) variable configuration. Refer to [Environment Setup and Management](#environment-setup-and-management) for more information.

The framework supports defining, managing, and evaluating research tasks. It uses a foundational interface for tasks, with implementations for question-answering datasets. A benchmark, [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14), offers a unified interface for assessing model responses against ground truth. The system also extracts novel tasks from scientific literature using LLM-based agents. Task management and evaluation details are in [Task Management and Evaluation](#task-management-and-evaluation).

## Project Overview and Core Components
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) project functions as an AI agent designed for autonomous biomedical research. It integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented planning and code execution to address problems within the biomedical domain. The system's architecture focuses on orchestrating various AI agents to manage research tasks, dynamically handle resources, and engage in conversational interactions to solve complex biomedical problems.

The core of [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) involves a sophisticated agent orchestration framework. The primary agent, [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56), manages the overall workflow, handling configuration, setting up LLMs, and dynamically managing tools and data. This agent's operational flow is built around a [`StateGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L15), which invokes LLMs for reasoning and executes code for practical tasks. Complementing [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56), a ReAct agent is implemented using [`LangGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L265) for managing conversational state, integrating LLMs, and invoking tools. This ReAct agent can dynamically register and configure tools, building its workflow to support reasoning, tool use, and retrieval.

LLM integration is a central component, allowing various LLMs from different providers to be configured and used. A factory function handles the instantiation of these models, supporting dynamic imports and provider-specific configurations. For executing research tasks, [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) includes a [`FunctionGenerator`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py#L22) agent that translates natural language into executable Python code. This agent leverages utility functions for safe and efficient execution, supporting languages like R and Bash.

Dynamic resource management and retrieval are key features, where the system intelligently selects relevant tools, data lake items, software libraries, and know-how documents. A [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8) utilizes LLM prompt-based selection to inform the agent's context, ensuring that the most appropriate resources are available for problem-solving. This dynamic approach enables the system to adapt to diverse biomedical queries and research scenarios.

### Biomni Agent (A1) Architecture and Workflow
The [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent, defined in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py), serves as the primary AI agent within the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework, orchestrating complex biomedical research tasks. Its architecture facilitates autonomous problem-solving through an interactive coding environment, dynamic tool and resource management, and comprehensive conversational logging.

The agent's workflow is managed by a [`StateGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L15), which defines a state machine to control the sequence of operations. This graph typically includes a [`generate`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L1381) node, responsible for invoking the underlying Large Language Model (LLM) to produce an action, and an [`execute`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L1471) node, which runs generated code in Python, R, or Bash environments. This design allows the [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent to iteratively plan, execute, and observe results, mimicking a human researcher's approach. Optional self-criticism capabilities can be integrated into this workflow, where an [`execute_self_critic`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L1579) node provides feedback to the LLM based on execution history, prompting for refinement or correction.

A core aspect of the [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent's functionality is its dynamic management of tools and resources. It can dynamically add new callable Python functions as tools, automatically generating API schemas and registering them for LLM use. Furthermore, it supports the integration of tools from external Multi-Component Protocol (MCP) servers, enabling the agent to extend its capabilities beyond its local environment. Beyond tools, the agent manages custom datasets and software libraries, incorporating them into the LLM's context. When [`use_tool_retriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/config.py#L40) is enabled, the agent leverages a [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8) to intelligently select relevant tools, data, libraries, and know-how documents based on the user's prompt, dynamically updating the system prompt provided to the LLM. This ensures that the LLM operates with a highly contextualized and relevant set of resources. For more information on resource management and retrieval, refer to [Dynamic Resource Management and Retrieval](#project-overview-and-core-components-dynamic-resource-management-and-retrieval).

The [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent integrates various components to support its operations. It interacts with LLMs for reasoning and code generation. For details on LLM integration, see [LLM Integration and Configuration](#project-overview-and-core-components-llm-integration-and-configuration). Code execution, a critical part of its workflow, involves running Python, R, or Bash scripts generated by the LLM, capturing outputs, and handling plots. This aspect is further detailed in [Code Generation and Execution](#project-overview-and-core-components-code-generation-and-execution).

Conversation history logging is another integral feature. The agent maintains a detailed log of interactions, including user prompts, LLM responses, code executions, and observations. This log can be exported as a PDF report, providing a comprehensive record for review, debugging, and reproducibility. This ensures transparency and traceability of the agent's autonomous research process. The [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent also manages resource loading based on [`commercial_mode`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/config.py#L43), accommodating different licensing requirements for datasets in academic versus commercial settings.

### ReAct Agent Implementation and State Management
The [`react`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L38) agent, implemented in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py), employs the ReAct (Reasoning and Acting) pattern within the [`LangGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L265) framework to address biomedical challenges. This design allows the agent to dynamically reason, execute tools, and observe results in an iterative cycle, forming a robust workflow for complex problem-solving.

Central to the agent's operation is its state management, handled by the [`AgentState`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L51) [`TypedDict`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L8). This structure primarily maintains a sequence of [`BaseMessage`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L12) objects, enabling the agent to track conversational history and internal thought processes. The [`add_messages`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L15) reducer within [`AgentState`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L51) ensures that the message sequence is consistently updated, reflecting the agent's evolving context.

The agent's ability to interact with its environment is facilitated by its dynamic tool management. During initialization, the [`react`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L38) agent loads available tools by reading API schemas from [`module2api`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L871) and converting them into [`LangChain`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L2196) compatible tools. A key design choice is the integration of a timeout mechanism for all tools via [`_add_timeout_to_tools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L90). This function wraps tool executions in a separate process, preventing any single tool from indefinitely blocking the agent's progress and enhancing overall system reliability. New tools can be dynamically added using the [`add_tool`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L225) method, which automatically generates API schemas from Python functions and applies the necessary timeout wrappers.

The agent's workflow is constructed using [`LangGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L265) within the [`_create_custom_react_agent`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L268) method. This workflow defines a cycle between calling the Language Model (LLM) and executing tools. The [`call_model`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L277) node invokes the LLM to determine the next action, while the [`tool_node`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L285) executes the tools suggested by the LLM. A conditional edge function, [`should_continue`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L310), governs the flow, allowing the agent to repeatedly reason and act until a final solution is reached. This [`StateGraph`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L15) setup provides a clear and manageable representation of the agent's decision-making process and execution path.

Furthermore, the [`react`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/react.py#L38) agent incorporates dynamic resource retrieval to optimize its problem-solving capabilities. When enabled, the [`go`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L1759) method utilizes a [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8) to intelligently select the most relevant tools, data lake items, and libraries based on the user's input. This prompt-based retrieval mechanism ensures that the LLM's context is enriched with only pertinent information, reducing cognitive load and improving the efficiency and accuracy of its responses. This selective resource integration allows the agent to adapt its capabilities to the specific demands of each biomedical query.

For a deeper understanding of the primary AI agent orchestrating problem-solving, refer to [Biomni Agent (A1) Architecture and Workflow](#project-overview-and-core-components-biomni-agent-a1-architecture-and-workflow). The overall approach to dynamic resource management and retrieval is further detailed in [Dynamic Resource Management and Retrieval](#project-overview-and-core-components-dynamic-resource-management-and-retrieval).

### LLM Integration and Configuration
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) project integrates various Large Language Models (LLMs) through a centralized system that supports multiple providers and offers flexible configuration options. This integration is primarily managed by the [`get_llm`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/llm.py#L13) factory function, located in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/llm.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/llm.py), which instantiates chat models from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Ollama, Gemini, and Bedrock.

Configuration for these LLMs can be managed through a hierarchy of settings, including environment variables, a [`default_config`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/config.py#L99) object, and direct parameters during agent instantiation. The [`BiomniConfig`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/config.py#L13) dataclass in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/config.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/config.py) centralizes these settings, allowing overrides from environment variables for flexible deployment. The [`get_llm`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/llm.py#L13) function automatically detects the LLM provider based on model names or environment variables and dynamically imports the necessary LangChain chat model classes. It also incorporates provider-specific logic, such as handling API quirks for newer OpenAI models or sourcing API keys from specific environment variables for Anthropic and Gemini. This modular approach ensures that the system can adapt to different LLM services and configurations while maintaining a consistent interface for the agents. For more details on overall project structure, refer to [Project Overview and Core Components](#project-overview-and-core-components).

### Code Generation and Execution
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) project incorporates a mechanism for generating and executing code from natural language descriptions, crucial for its autonomous research capabilities. The central component for code generation is the [`FunctionGenerator`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py#L22) agent, defined in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py). This agent translates a given task description into executable Python code, ensuring the output adheres to specific formatting requirements.

The [`FunctionGenerator`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py#L22) utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) to perform the translation. It constructs a system prompt that guides the LLM to generate Python code within a triple-backtick block, including minimal comments, and avoiding unnecessary external dependencies. The agent then extracts the generated code from the LLM's response using regular expressions and determines a safe and descriptive filename for the script.

For the execution of generated code, [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) provides a suite of utility functions, primarily located in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py). These utilities support various programming languages and command-line interfaces:
*   [`run_r_code`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L25) executes R code scripts.
*   [`run_bash_script`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L56) runs Bash scripts.
*   [`run_cli_command`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L148) executes single command-line interface commands.
*   [`run_with_timeout`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L183) allows for executing any function with a specified time limit, terminating the process if it exceeds the allocated time.

These execution utilities abstract away the complexities of interacting with external environments, such as setting up temporary files for scripts, handling standard output and error streams, and ensuring proper process termination. This robust execution framework is essential for the [`A1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L56) agent, described in [Biomni Agent (A1) Architecture and Workflow](#project-overview-and-core-components-biomni-agent-a1-architecture-and-workflow), as it allows the agent to dynamically execute code and adapt its workflow based on intermediate results, enabling autonomous problem-solving in biomedical research. The [`FunctionGenerator`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/function_generator.py#L22) itself is also utilized in processes such as the extraction of tasks from bioRxiv papers, as detailed in [LLM-based Task Extraction from BioRxiv Papers](#task-management-and-evaluation-llm-based-task-extraction-from-biorxiv-papers), where it helps to create Python functions based on identified tasks.

### Dynamic Resource Management and Retrieval
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) agent dynamically manages and retrieves various resources, including tools, data lake items, software libraries, and know-how documents. This dynamic handling allows the agent to adapt its capabilities to the specific task at hand, leveraging external knowledge and computational power as needed. The core mechanism for this is the [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8), which uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to select the most relevant resources based on a user's query, thereby informing the agent's context.

The process begins when an agent receives a query or prompt. Rather than having a fixed set of capabilities, the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) agent can intelligently scan a vast collection of available resources. These resources are comprehensively described in metadata repositories, such as [`data_lake_dict`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L2) and [`library_content_dict`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L82) found in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py), which detail biomedical datasets and computational tools, respectively. For commercial applications, a curated version, [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc_cm.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc_cm.py), filters resources based on licensing. Structured know-how documents, like those detailing sgRNA design or single-cell RNA-seq annotation in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how), also form a crucial part of this resource pool.

The [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8) in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py) plays a central role. It takes the user's query and the descriptions of all available resources, then formulates a detailed prompt for an LLM. This prompt guides the LLM to understand the user's intent and identify which tools, datasets, software libraries, or know-how documents are most pertinent. The LLM's response, typically a list of indices corresponding to the selected resources, is then parsed by the retriever. This allows the agent to efficiently narrow down its operational scope and equip itself with only the necessary components, enhancing both relevance and computational efficiency. The retrieved resources subsequently update the agent's system prompt, ensuring the LLM's reasoning is grounded in the most relevant context and available capabilities. This mechanism allows the agent to dynamically integrate information from external sources, execute code, and leverage specialized knowledge to solve complex biomedical problems.

## Biomedical Tools and Resources
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework provides a wide array of tools and resources for biological and medical analyses. These resources are dynamically managed and retrieved to support autonomous research tasks. A core component of this system is the intelligent selection of relevant tools and information, driven by Large Language Models (LLMs). This allows the system to effectively respond to user queries by identifying and utilizing the most appropriate resources from its extensive collection.

The system incorporates a comprehensive suite of biomedical tools, organized by scientific discipline within the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool) directory. These tools cover areas such as biochemistry, bioengineering, bioimaging, cancer biology, cell biology, genomics, immunology, molecular biology, and microbiology. Each tool is designed to perform specific analytical tasks, ranging from protein sequence analysis and enzyme kinetics to advanced image processing and genomic sequencing interpretation. For example, tools in biochemistry can analyze circular dichroism spectra, while bioimaging tools leverage [`nnUNet`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L32) for segmentation and [`SimpleITK`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L11) for image registration. [Comprehensive Biomedical Tool Suite](#biomedical-tools-and-resources-comprehensive-biomedical-tool-suite) provides a more detailed overview of these specialized tools.

Beyond analytical tools, [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) also manages a rich collection of structured know-how documents and protocols. These include detailed guides, such as those for sgRNA design in CRISPR experiments and best practices for single-cell RNA-seq cell type annotation, which are stored as Markdown files within the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how) directory. This structured knowledge is crucial for guiding the AI agent in complex experimental design and data interpretation tasks. [Know-How Documents and Protocols](#biomedical-tools-and-resources-know-how-documents-and-protocols) offers further details on these documents.

The dynamic retrieval of these resources is handled by the [`ToolRetriever`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py#L8) class, primarily found in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/model/retriever.py). This class uses LLM prompt-based selection to interpret user queries and determine which tools, data lake items, software libraries, or know-how documents are most relevant. The LLM is given detailed descriptions of available resources and explicit instructions to select those pertinent to the query, effectively translating natural language requests into actionable resource selections. This enables the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) agent to maintain context and adapt its capabilities based on the specific biomedical problem at hand. [Dynamic Resource Management and Retrieval](#project-overview-and-core-components-dynamic-resource-management-and-retrieval) further explains this process.

Additionally, the framework integrates specialized tools for laboratory automation and literature research. This includes tools for interacting with laboratory robotics platforms like PyLabRobot, enabling dynamic access to documentation and script testing. For academic research, the system offers tools to search and extract content from databases such as PubMed and arXiv, and to perform advanced web searches, enhancing the agent's ability to gather information from scientific literature. [Lab Automation and Literature Tools](#biomedical-tools-and-resources-lab-automation-and-literature-tools) describes these functionalities in more detail.

### Tool Descriptions and Domains
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) project employs a structured metadata system to define and categorize its extensive collection of biological and medical tools. This system, primarily located under the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description) directory, allows for programmatic discovery, invocation, and validation of tool functionalities. Tool descriptions are organized by scientific discipline, with dedicated Python files for areas such as biochemistry ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/biochemistry.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/biochemistry.py)), bioengineering ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/bioengineering.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/bioengineering.py)), genomics ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/genomics.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/genomics.py)), immunology ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/immunology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/immunology.py)), and pharmacology ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/pharmacology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/tool_description/pharmacology.py)).

Each tool is described using a dictionary that specifies its purpose, a unique programmatic name, and detailed specifications for its input parameters. Parameters are categorized as either required or optional, with each entry defining its name, type (e.g., [`str`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/llm.py#L10), [`int`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L262), [`List[str]`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L550)), a human-readable description, and a default value if applicable. This standardized format enables automated systems to understand a tool's capabilities, dynamically generate user interfaces for input, and validate provided arguments before execution.

For instance, tools for biochemical analysis, such as [`analyze_circular_dichroism_spectra`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py#L1), define required inputs like [`sample_name`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1483) and [`wavelength_data`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py#L4), alongside optional ones like [`temperature_data`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py#L6). Similarly, the [`annotate_celltype_scRNA`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L463) tool specifies various optional parameters for customization. This consistent metadata structure is crucial for the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) agent's ability to orchestrate complex research tasks by dynamically selecting and executing the appropriate tools based on the problem at hand, as discussed further in [Dynamic Resource Management and Retrieval](#project-overview-and-core-components-dynamic-resource-management-and-retrieval).

### Comprehensive Biomedical Tool Suite
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework includes a suite of tools for various biological and medical analyses, categorized by scientific discipline. These tools perform tasks ranging from biochemical data interpretation to complex genomic and cell biology analyses, integrating with external libraries and services.

**Biochemistry** tools, located in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py), analyze diverse biochemical data. They process circular dichroism spectra to determine protein secondary structure and thermal stability, analyze RNA secondary structures from dot-bracket notation, and fit enzyme kinetics data to models like [`michaelis_menten`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py#L372) to derive parameters such as [`vmax`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py#L372) and [`km`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biochemistry.py#L319). Additionally, these tools analyze ITC data to quantify binding thermodynamics and perform protein conservation analysis through sequence alignment using [`MuscleCommandline`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py#L1478) and phylogenetic tree construction.

**Bioengineering** tools, defined in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py), handle data for bioengineering applications. They quantify cell migration metrics from time-lapse microscopy using [`tp.locate`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L59) and [`tp.link_df`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L75), simulate CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, and analyze neuronal activity from GCaMP imaging data by detecting events and fitting [`exp_decay`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L498). Other functions analyze drug release kinetics by fitting models such as [`zero_order`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L658) and [`higuchi`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L664), quantify myofiber morphology using [`skimage`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L374) functions like [`filters.threshold_otsu`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L655), and decode behavioral variables from neural trajectories using [`PCA`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L1088) and [`KalmanFilter`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioengineering.py#L1087). The toolkit also simulates whole-cell ODE models with [`solve_ivp`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/physiology.py#L1129).

**Bioimaging** functionalities, housed in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py), provide medical image processing capabilities, particularly for segmentation and registration. The [`SegmentationTool`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L30) manages [`nnUNet`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L32)-based segmentation, including splitting modalities, preparing input for [`nnUNet`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L32), and handling model downloads and environment setup. The [`ImageRegistrationTool`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L579) offers [`SimpleITK`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/bioimaging.py#L11)-based image registration, encompassing image loading, preprocessing, and the creation of rigid, affine, and deformable transforms, along with similarity metric calculations.

**Biophysics** tools, found in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biophysics.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biophysics.py), address biophysical analyses such as predicting intrinsically disordered regions in proteins, analyzing cell morphology and cytoskeletal organization from fluorescence microscopy images using [`skimage`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L374) and [`cv2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L24), and quantifying tissue deformation and flow dynamics from image sequences through [`cv2.calcOpticalFlowPyrLK`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biophysics.py#L402).

**Cancer Biology** analysis tools, within [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py), perform various tasks related to cancer research. They reconstruct and analyze DNA Damage Response (DDR) networks using [`pearsonr`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/physiology.py#L431) for interactions and [`degree_centrality`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py#L138) for identifying hub genes, quantify cell senescence and apoptosis from flow cytometry data using [`FCMeasurement`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L1010) and gating, and detect and annotate somatic mutations by orchestrating external tools like [`gatk Mutect2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py#L427) and [`snpEff`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py#L515). Other capabilities include detecting structural variations using [`lumpyexpress`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py#L677) and [`bcftools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cancer_biology.py#L705), applying Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to gene expression data for tumor subtyping, and analyzing copy number variations and tumor purity with tools like [`cnvkit`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/docs/known_conflicts.md#L16).

**Cell Biology** functions, located in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cell_biology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cell_biology.py), perform cell-level analyses. These include quantifying cell cycle phases from microscopy images, tracking cell motility and clustering patterns using [`KMeans`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/cell_biology.py#L185), simulating FACS-based cell sorting, and immunophenotyping flow cytometry data with [`FlowCytometryTools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L1001). Additionally, they quantify mitochondrial morphology and membrane potential from paired fluorescence microscopy images.

**Genetics** tools, detailed in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py), provide utilities for genomic and genetic analysis. These tools perform genomic coordinate liftover using [`pyliftover`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L91), implement Bayesian fine-mapping with deep variational inference, analyze CRISPR-Cas9 mutation outcomes by sequence alignment with [`pairwise2.align.globalms`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py#L391), and simulate demographic histories using [`msprime`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L160). They also identify transcription factor binding sites using JASPAR PWMs, fit genomic prediction models using linear mixed models, and simulate PCR and gel electrophoresis. Protein phylogeny analysis is performed using [`MuscleCommandline`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py#L1478) and [`iqtree`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py#L1465).

**Genomics** capabilities, in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py), include various bioinformatics tools for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis, gene annotation, and genomic interaction analysis. These tools facilitate unsupervised cell type transfer between scRNA-seq datasets using [`popv`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L43), interspecies gene conversion via [`pybiomart`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L12), and the generation of gene embeddings with ESM models. Cell type annotation in scRNA-seq data is supported through [`leiden`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L468) clustering and LLM-based prediction, as well as hierarchical annotation using [`panhumanpy`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L108). The toolkit also generates [`scvi`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L98) and [`harmony`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L130) embeddings, maps cells to the IMA reference, fetches RNA-seq data from ARCHS4 using [`gget.archs4`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L992), and performs gene set enrichment analysis with [`gget.enrichr`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1061). Other functions analyze Hi-C data for chromatin interactions, perform comparative genomics using [`bwa`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L198), call ChIP-seq peaks with [`macs2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L291), discover motifs with [`HOMER`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L1803), and analyze genomic region overlaps using [`pybedtools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L107). It also generates State embeddings for single-cell RNA-seq data using the SE-600M model.

**Glycoengineering** utilities, in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/glycoengineering.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/glycoengineering.py), focus on analyzing protein sequences for glycosylation motifs and hotspots. These functions, designed to be dependency-light, scan for N-linked glycosylation sequons and predict O-glycosylation hotspots based on serine/threonine density.

**Immunology** tools, within [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py), analyze immunology-related experimental data. They orchestrate ATAC-seq differential accessibility pipelines using [`macs2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L291), analyze bacterial growth curves by fitting [`logistic_growth`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L224) models, and simulate immune cell isolation and purification, including MACS. Functions also estimate cell cycle phase durations from flow cytometry data using [`minimize`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L584) and [`simulate_cell_population`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L529), track immune cells under flow conditions using [`cv2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L24) and [`trackpy`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L149), and quantify CFSE cell proliferation using [`FlowCytometryTools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L1001). Further analyses include quantifying cytokine production in CD4+ T cells, analyzing EBV antibody titers from ELISA data, and analyzing CNS lesion histology and immunohistochemistry images using [`scikit-image`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L283).

**Microbiology** analysis and simulation tools are available in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/microbiology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/microbiology.py). They optimize anaerobic digestion processes, analyze arsenic speciation, count bacterial colonies from images using [`cv2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L24), annotate bacterial genomes with [`prokka`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/microbiology.py#L537), and enumerate bacterial CFU by serial dilution. These tools also model bacterial growth dynamics using [`logistic_growth`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/immunology.py#L224) ODEs, quantify biofilm biomass, segment and analyze microbial cells using [`skimage`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L374) functions like [`watershed`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/pathology.py#L833) and [`measure.regionprops_table`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/biophysics.py#L202), and simulate generalized Lotka-Volterra dynamics using [`odeint`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/microbiology.py#L1295). RNA secondary structure prediction with ViennaRNA's [`RNA.fold`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/microbiology.py#L1383) and microbial population dynamics simulation using the Gillespie algorithm are also supported.

**Molecular Biology** operations are performed by tools in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/molecular_biology.py). These include annotating open reading frames, annotating plasmids using external tools like [`plannotate`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L217), retrieving gene coding sequences and plasmid sequences from NCBI Entrez and Addgene, aligning sequences using [`pairwise2`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genetics.py#L351), and simulating PCR and restriction enzyme digestion. They also find restriction sites, identify restriction enzymes, detect sequence mutations, design knockout sgRNAs, and design various primers for PCR, Golden Gate assembly, and Sanger sequencing. Additionally, the framework can generate step-by-step laboratory protocols.

The framework also includes dedicated modules for database querying, lab automation, and literature searching. The **Database** tools in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/database.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/database.py) facilitate querying biological and medical databases like UniProt, AlphaFold, InterPro, PDB, KEGG, STRING, and others by translating natural language prompts into structured API calls via an LLM. **Lab Automation** tools, located in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/lab_automation.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/lab_automation.py), provide utilities for PyLabRobot documentation access and script testing in a simulated environment. The **Literature** tools in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/literature.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/literature.py) support academic research by enabling queries to [`arxiv`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L142), Google Scholar, PubMed, and general web searches, as well as extracting content from URLs and PDFs. An example [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L2004) service for PubMed is provided in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py) for searching articles and retrieving abstracts.

### Know-How Documents and Protocols
Markdown-based know-how documents are managed through the [`KnowHowLoader`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/loader.py#L8) class, primarily implemented in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/loader.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/loader.py), which is exposed via [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/__init__.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/__init__.py). This system parses Markdown files to extract content, titles, descriptions, and structured metadata, making them programmatically accessible to agents. Key documents include guides for sgRNA design and single-cell RNA-seq cell type annotation. The sgRNA design guide, located at [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/sgRNA_design_guide.md`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/sgRNA_design_guide.md), provides a three-tiered approach for obtaining sgRNA sequences, prioritizing validated sequences, then pre-computed datasets from sources like CRISPick, and finally de novo design guidelines. It details methods for searching curated databases, performing advanced web searches, and utilizing data from external resources. The single-cell RNA-seq cell type annotation guide, found at [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/single_cell_annotation.md`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/single_cell_annotation.md), outlines best practices for annotating cell types in single-cell RNA-seq data. It covers manual marker-based annotation, automated annotation using pre-trained classifiers, and reference-based label transfer, offering a recommended workflow, practical tips, common pitfalls, and a tool selection guide. Supporting resources, such as CRISPR experiment data downloads from [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/resource/CRISPick_download_links.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/know_how/resource/CRISPick_download_links.txt), are also integrated into this system.

An extensive collection of laboratory protocols is also available, primarily housed within [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols). These protocols cover a broad spectrum of molecular biology, cell biology, and general laboratory techniques, sourced largely from Addgene and Thermo Fisher Scientific. These detailed instructions guide users through experimental procedures, sample preparation, and analytical methods. For instance, the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene) directory contains protocols for viral vector production (AAV and lentivirus), including detailed steps for AAV production ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV Production.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV Production.txt)), purification ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV Purification.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV Purification.txt)), and titration using qPCR ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV Titration by qPCR.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV Titration by qPCR.txt)) or ddPCR ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV ddPCR Titration.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ AAV ddPCR Titration.txt)). It also includes protocols for nucleic acid manipulation, such as general mammalian cell transfection ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ General Transfection.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ General Transfection.txt)), various cloning techniques (e.g., Gibson Assembly in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Gibson Assembly Protocol.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Gibson Assembly Protocol.txt) and Ligation Independent Cloning in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Ligation Independent Cloning.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Ligation Independent Cloning.txt)), and DNA/RNA purification. Furthermore, protocols for antibody purification and validation (e.g., indirect ELISA in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Antibody Validation Using the Indirect ELISA Method.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Antibody Validation Using the Indirect ELISA Method.txt) and affinity purification in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Affinity Purification of Recombinant Antibodies with Protein A or Protein G.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/addgene/Addgene_ Affinity Purification of Recombinant Antibodies with Protein A or Protein G.txt)) and cell line isolation are provided.

The [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher) subdirectory focuses on cell biology techniques, encompassing cell culture, proliferation, viability, apoptosis, and microscopy sample preparation. This includes guidelines for adherent and suspension cell culture, cell freezing, various cell dissociation methods, and a range of assays for cell proliferation (e.g., BrdU labeling in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/BrdU Labeling & Detection Protocol _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/BrdU Labeling & Detection Protocol _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt)), viability (e.g., Trypan Blue Exclusion in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/Trypan Blue Exclusion _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/Trypan Blue Exclusion _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt)), and apoptosis (e.g., Annexin V staining in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/BestProtocols_ Annexin V Staining Protocol for Flow Cytometry _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/BestProtocols_ Annexin V Staining Protocol for Flow Cytometry _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt)). Immunostaining protocols for targets like actin ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/Actin Staining Protocol _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/Actin Staining Protocol _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt)), nuclear staining ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/DAPI Protocol for Fluorescence Imaging _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/DAPI Protocol for Fluorescence Imaging _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt)), and specific instructions for staining 3D cell cultures ([`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/Staining 3D Cell Cultures for Imaging _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/protocols/thermofisher/Staining 3D Cell Cultures for Imaging _ Thermo Fisher Scientific - US.txt)) are also available, alongside ELISA and protein quantification methods.

### Lab Automation and Literature Tools
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework incorporates specialized tools for interacting with literature databases and facilitating lab automation. For academic research, the system offers functionality to search and retrieve information from platforms like PubMed. An example of this capability is demonstrated by the services provided in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py), which exposes methods for searching PubMed articles and retrieving their abstracts. This is achieved by utilizing the Entrez library to communicate with NCBI databases. The data is structured using [`BaseModel`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L21) to define article information, ensuring consistency and validation. For instance, the [`search_pubmed`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L20) tool performs a query, returning structured [`Article`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L11) objects containing details such as PMID, title, journal, and year, while the [`get_article_abstract`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L32) tool retrieves the abstract for a specified article. These tools are registered as callable services using [`FastMCP`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/a1.py#L2004), enabling their remote invocation and integration into broader research workflows. While the description of lab automation tools, such as dynamic documentation access and script testing for PyLabRobot, is mentioned in the overall plan, the provided summaries do not contain specific details for this aspect within [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools).

## Environment Setup and Management
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) project requires a specialized bioinformatics environment for its operations. This environment is orchestrated through a set of shell scripts located in the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env) directory, designed to manage [`conda`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L30) and [`micromamba`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L21) installations, integrate core bioinformatics tools, install R packages, and configure command-line interface (CLI) tools. The environment setup process handles error conditions and ensures proper environment activation and [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) variable configuration.

The primary script for setting up the environment is [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh). This script verifies the presence of either [`conda`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L30) or [`micromamba`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L21) and uses them to install various environments from YAML configuration files. These include a base [`biomni_e1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L43) environment, core bioinformatics tools, and R packages. The script also handles the installation of additional R packages via [`Rscript`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L41). A core functionality of [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh) is its error handling, which provides robust error management and allows for both interactive and non-interactive installation modes. Upon completion, the script provides guidance on how to activate the environment and configure system [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) variables.

Managing command-line interface (CLI) tools is handled by the specialized script [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh). This script installs and configures bioinformatics tools such as PLINK and IQ-TREE, managing their installation directory and ensuring they are accessible via the system's [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147). It supports adding new tools via a [`cli_tools_config.json`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L144) file and includes mechanisms for persistent [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) configuration across shell sessions. For more details on this process, see [Managing Command-Line Interface (CLI) Tools](#environment-setup-and-management-managing-command-line-interface-cli-tools).

For incremental updates and the installation of new software packages and libraries, the project utilizes scripts like [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/new_software_v008.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/new_software_v008.sh). This script automates the installation of various Python packages using [`pip`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L46) and [`uv`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L2211), handles [`git-lfs`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L2211) setup for large files, and integrates [`conda`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L30) installations for specific tools like [`weasyprint`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L234). This modular approach ensures that the environment can be updated efficiently with new dependencies. Further details on this process are available in [Incremental Software Updates and Version Management](#environment-setup-and-management-incremental-software-updates-and-version-management).

The [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/README.md`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/README.md) file serves as a comprehensive guide for users, detailing different installation options based on desired functionality and resource constraints. It covers basic environment setup, full [`E1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L40) environment configuration, and specialized environments for tasks like copy number analysis. It also provides instructions for activating environments and adding support for additional [`langchain`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L180) packages.

### Orchestrating the Environment Setup with `setup.sh`
The primary orchestration script for setting up the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) environment is [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh). This script automates the installation of various components necessary for the biomedical AI agent, including Conda/micromamba environments, core bioinformatics tools, R packages, and command-line interface (CLI) tools. The process begins with verifying the presence of either [`conda`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L30) or [`micromamba`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L21), ensuring the foundational package management system is available.

The script manages environment installations from YAML files, such as [`environment.yml`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L60) for the base [`biomni_e1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L43) environment, [`bio_env.yml`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L60) for core bioinformatics tools, and [`r_packages.yml`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L61) for R packages. It integrates CLI tools by invoking [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh), which handles the specific installation and PATH configuration for tools like PLINK and IQ-TREE. The script also includes error handling mechanisms to manage installation failures and supports both interactive and non-interactive modes, allowing for either guided setup or automated deployment. After installation, it provides instructions for activating the environment and correctly configuring the system's PATH. For a detailed discussion of the CLI tool management, see [Managing Command-Line Interface (CLI) Tools](#environment-setup-and-management-managing-command-line-interface-cli-tools).

### Managing Command-Line Interface (CLI) Tools
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) environment setup includes robust mechanisms for installing and managing command-line interface (CLI) bioinformatics tools. This functionality is primarily handled by the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh) script, which orchestrates the download, installation, and configuration of various tools such as [`PLINK`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L291) and [`IQ-TREE`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L291).

The [`install_cli_tools.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L62) script automates the process of obtaining these tools, often involving fetching binaries, compiling source code, or executing specialized installers. It ensures that the tools are placed in a designated [`biomni_tools`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/MANIFEST.in#L9) directory and that their executables are discoverable by the system through proper [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) variable configuration. This configuration includes adding the tools' binary directory to the current shell session's [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) and persistently modifying user profile files (e.g., [`.bashrc`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh#L550), [`.zshrc`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/install_cli_tools.sh#L555)) to maintain access across sessions. To simplify this, a [`setup_path.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L63) script is generated to manage [`PATH`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L147) modifications.

A key design choice for tool management is the use of a configuration-driven approach. Tool metadata, including download Uniform Resource Locators (URLs), expected binary paths, and commands for version verification, are stored in a [`cli_tools_config.json`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L144) file. This allows for flexible addition and updating of new tools without altering the core script logic. The script is also platform-aware, differentiating between Linux, macOS Intel, and macOS ARM64 architectures to retrieve the correct binaries. The overall environment setup is detailed further in [Orchestrating the Environment Setup with `setup.sh`](#environment-setup-and-management-orchestrating-the-environment-setup-with-setupsh).

### Incremental Software Updates and Version Management
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework facilitates incremental updates and installations of software packages and libraries to manage its evolving dependencies. This process is primarily handled by shell scripts designed to add new software components to an existing environment without requiring a full reinstallation.

For instance, the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/new_software_v008.sh`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/new_software_v008.sh) script automates the installation of dependencies specific to Biomni version 0.0.8. This script uses a combination of package managers:
*   [`pip`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L46) is extensively used for Python packages such as [`transformers`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/fixed_env.yml#L705), [`sentencepiece`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/fixed_env.yml#L647), [`langchain-google-genai`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/README.md#L72), [`langchain_ollama`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/llm.py#L229), and [`mcp`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/example_mcp_tools/pubmed_mcp.py#L8). It also supports direct installations from Git repositories, as seen with [`popV`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L46) and [`pylabrobot`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/env_desc.py#L220).
*   [`uv`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L2211), a faster Python package installer, is employed for certain packages like [`transcriptformer`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L2443) and [`arc-state`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L2211), indicating an adoption of more efficient dependency management tools.
*   [`conda`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni_env/setup.sh#L30) is utilized for packages that might have complex dependencies or are better managed within the Conda ecosystem, such as [`weasyprint`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L234).
*   System-level installations, like [`git-lfs`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/tool/genomics.py#L2211), are managed to handle large files often associated with scientific datasets and models.

This approach allows for flexible and targeted updates, ensuring that the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) environment remains current with its software requirements while minimizing the overhead of full environment rebuilds. For a comprehensive overview of environment setup, refer to [Environment Setup and Management](#environment-setup-and-management).

## Task Management and Evaluation
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework provides a structured approach to defining, managing, and evaluating various research tasks, particularly those involving question answering and information extraction within the biomedical domain. This system enables the agent to interact with diverse datasets and assess its performance against established benchmarks.

At its core, [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) uses a foundational interface for tasks, defined in [`base_task.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L92), which specifies abstract methods for task initialization, example retrieval, data iteration, and evaluation. This interface ensures consistency across different task implementations. Concrete examples include handling multiple-choice question datasets, such as "Humanity's Last Exam" (HLE) as implemented in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py) and biology-related questions in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/lab_bench.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/lab_bench.py). These implementations manage data loading from parquet files, process questions and answer choices, generate prompts for language models, and evaluate responses based on metrics like accuracy, coverage, and precision. The output is structured using Pydantic [`BaseModel`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L21)s, ensuring consistency for downstream processing.

For evaluating the agent's performance, the [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14) benchmark, detailed in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py), offers a unified interface. This class loads a comprehensive dataset of task instances and provides methods to evaluate user answers against ground truth. The [`_compute_reward`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L71) method within [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14) encapsulates task-specific scoring logic, which can vary from simple string comparisons for tasks like CRISPR delivery and GWAS variant prioritization to complex JSON parsing for rare disease diagnosis or patient gene detection. This modular design allows for the extension of evaluation criteria to accommodate new types of biomedical problems.

Beyond predefined benchmarks, [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) also incorporates capabilities for extracting novel tasks directly from scientific literature. Scripts located in the [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts) directory, such as [`extract_biorxiv_tasks.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L84), leverage LLM-based agents to analyze bioRxiv papers. This process involves downloading PDFs, extracting text, and then identifying common tasks, databases, and software mentioned within the papers. The extracted information is then summarized, generating insights into emerging research areas and potential new tasks for the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) agent. Furthermore, the [`generate_function.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L85) script in the same directory demonstrates how these extracted task descriptions can be used to generate Python functions automatically, facilitating the expansion of the agent's capabilities.

### Foundational Task Interface and Implementations
The [`base_task`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/base_task.py#L1) abstract interface provides a standardized structure for various tasks within the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework. This interface, defined in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/base_task.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/base_task.py), requires implementations for task initialization, example retrieval, iteration over datasets, and evaluation of results. A key method, [`get_prompt_from_input`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/base_task.py#L17), offers a default mechanism for generating prompts by expecting a "prompt" key from the [`get_example`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py#L103) method, thus streamlining prompt creation across different tasks.

Concrete implementations of this interface include tasks for multiple-choice question datasets. For instance, the [`humanity_last_exam`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py#L14) class in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py) handles questions from the "Humanity's Last Exam" dataset. It loads and filters data from a Parquet file, extracts questions and correct letter answers, and provides methods to retrieve individual examples or iterate through the entire dataset. This class also defines an [`evaluate`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py#L119) method to calculate metrics such as accuracy, coverage, and precision for model responses, and specifies a Pydantic [`BaseModel`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L21) for structured output.

Similarly, the [`lab_bench`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/lab_bench.py#L14) class in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/lab_bench.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/lab_bench.py) manages multiple-choice biology questions from another Parquet dataset. It loads and processes question data, dynamically shuffles options (including a "Insufficient information" choice), and formats prompts with specific tags to guide language model responses. Like [`humanity_last_exam`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py#L14), it offers example retrieval, iteration, and an [`evaluate`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/task/hle.py#L119) method to assess model performance with metrics like accuracy, coverage, and refrain ratio. It also utilizes a Pydantic [`BaseModel`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/utils.py#L21) for structured parsing of model outputs, ensuring consistency in how results are handled.

### BiomniEval1 Benchmark Evaluation Utilities
The [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14) class provides a unified interface for evaluating responses to various tasks within the BiomniEval1 benchmark. Its primary role is to load a dataset of benchmark tasks and their ground truth, and then to compute a score for a given user answer. This class, defined in [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py), is made accessible via [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/__init__.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/__init__.py).

At its core, [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14) loads the benchmark dataset, which contains information about different tasks, including prompts, ground truth answers, and unique identifiers. It optimizes lookup of individual task instances, allowing for quick retrieval of specific problems and their corresponding correct answers.

The evaluation process is handled by methods that compare a user's generated answer against the established ground truth. This comparison is not one-size-fits-all; instead, [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14) employs task-specific logic to calculate rewards. For some tasks, evaluation might involve simple string comparisons, while others, particularly those requiring structured outputs, might necessitate parsing JSON objects or evaluating complex data structures to identify correctness. This flexible approach accommodates the diverse range of problems presented in the biomedical domain, from factual recall to complex diagnostic reasoning.

Beyond evaluating individual answers, the [`BiomniEval1`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/eval/biomni_eval1.py#L14) class also offers utilities for retrieving task-related information. Users can list all available tasks, query statistics about the dataset (such as the number of instances per task or split), and retrieve specific instances or subsets of instances for a given task. This facilitates not only the evaluation of AI agents but also the exploration and understanding of the benchmark itself. For a broader view of task management within the [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework, refer to [Foundational Task Interface and Implementations](#task-management-and-evaluation-foundational-task-interface-and-implementations).

### LLM-based Task Extraction from BioRxiv Papers
The [`biomni`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/README.md#L25) framework includes functionality to automatically extract structured information from bioRxiv pre-print papers, converting scientific text into actionable data such as tasks, databases, and software mentioned within the research. This process is driven by Large Language Models (LLMs) and is designed to streamline the discovery of research methodologies and resources.

The core workflow for extracting information from bioRxiv papers is orchestrated by the [`extract_biorxiv_tasks.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/DETAILS.md#L84) script, located at [`/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts/extract_biorxiv_tasks.py`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts/extract_biorxiv_tasks.py). This script begins by parsing command-line arguments that define parameters such as the subject area of interest, the number of papers to process, the specific LLM to use, and output directories. It then loads bioRxiv metadata from a CSV file, filtering papers based on specified subjects and publication status.

For each selected paper, the system downloads its PDF using [`download_pdf`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts/extract_biorxiv_tasks.py#L122) and extracts the textual content from it via [`extract_text_from_pdf`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts/extract_biorxiv_tasks.py#L159). To manage the input size for the LLM, the extracted text is truncated by [`truncate_text`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts/extract_biorxiv_tasks.py#L181) while attempting to preserve sentence integrity. The crucial step of information extraction is performed by an external [`PaperTaskExtractor`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/agent/env_collection.py#L12) agent, which processes the paper's text to identify and categorize tasks, databases, and software. The results for each paper are saved as individual JSON files. Finally, [`generate_summary`](https://github.com/snap-stanford/biomni/biomni/biorxiv_scripts/extract_biorxiv_tasks.py#L292) aggregates these individual extractions into comprehensive summaries, including CSV files for each category and a JSON file detailing the frequency of each unique entity. The design of this script emphasizes modularity, external LLM agent utilization, idempotency for resuming interrupted processes, and extensive command-line configurability.
